name: Fatima Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Bauer family on their farm out past the chapel. They milk about a hundred and fifty goats, make cheese in a little dairy in the yard, and grow apples and some wheat and oats. I help with the milking at six, then wash down, then most days I'm in the cheese room turning and salting the wheels, or out in the orchard. Mrs Bauer makes the cheese, I'm her pair of hands while I learn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. I stayed home with Sofia and Luca while they were small, then I did a year at the bakery counter in the supermarket, and I hated it. The Bauers go to our church and they needed help, so here I am at forty-three, still making mistakes with the curd. Paolo drives a lorry, long distance, so he's away three nights a week. The money's tight, we've got the mortgage and maybe two weeks saved, but I feel useful there in a way I never did at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now maybe people will look up from their phones. I'd say it after Mass, probably, and everyone would laugh because I'm always saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay as they are, which I'd take gladly. Sofia uses the chatbot for her homework, and sometimes she gets it to write my shopping list, and that's fine. A cheese doesn't care how clever your phone is, it cares if you turned it on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the Bauers' and keep learning the cheese. Maybe ask Mrs Bauer if I can start making one batch on my own each week. Keep a close eye on money like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Paolo think about AI and his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He hears about self-driving lorries on the radio all day. He says they'll never manage the mountain roads in snow. I hope he's right, but he also said that about the satnav.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pinch like now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We manage, just. The boiler is making a noise I don't like. If it goes, it goes on the credit card and we pay it off for a year.

S0.say: She'd say that with AI fading, maybe people would look up from their phones. She'd say this after Mass, where friends know it's her familiar line.
S0.think: Privately she'd gladly take things staying as they are. She uses AI only when her daughter sets it up, and her cheese work doesn't depend on it.
S0.do: Keeps working on the goat dairy farm and keeps learning cheesemaking. Asks to make one batch on her own each week and watches money closely.
S0.quote: A cheese doesn't care how clever your phone is, it cares if you turned it on Thursday.
S0.fieldNote: Her work gives her a sense of being useful that a supermarket job didn't. Her partner's lorry job is a quiet second exposure she already notices. Church community links her to her employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll manage, families always have. It's a change, like any other, and you do the work in front of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it frightens me because of Paolo, not me. Robot milking is already here, so the Bauers might buy one, but the cheese still needs a person for now. The lorries, though, I think they'll go one road at a time, and he's the earner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start selling my own apple chutney and jams at the Saturday market, I've wanted to for years, maybe fifty a week. I'd cut the satellite television and the kids' magazine subscriptions. I'd let Sofia show me how to use the AI properly for the market labels and costings, since she's always offering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be counting things at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jars, money, days until Paolo's home. Silly things. When I can't sleep I count how many jars of chutney pay one month of the mortgage. It's four hundred and twelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want help from the government if Paolo's work went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want help to find him new work, not money for nothing. My father would turn in his grave. But I'd take help for the children if it came to it, children come before pride.

S1.say: She'd say families will manage as they always have. She'd frame it as change like any other, where you do the work in front of you.
S1.think: Privately she's frightened mainly for her partner, the main earner, whose lorry work could be automated road by road. Cheesemaking still needs a person for now.
S1.do: Starts selling her own apple chutney and jams at the Saturday market for about fifty a week. Cuts satellite TV and the children's magazines, and lets her daughter teach her AI for labels and costings.
S1.quote: When I can't sleep I count how many jars of chutney pay one month of the mortgage. It's four hundred and twelve.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is driven by her partner's exposure more than her own. She'd accept help for the children but wants work rather than money for adults. Her steady adoption runs through her daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to pray, and we need to look after each other, because nobody in power saw this coming. I'd want the church running a food bank by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be in real trouble. Paolo's lorry goes, robots milk the goats, and maybe a machine can even turn a cheese. Two weeks of savings and a mortgage, with both of us out at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the priest and my brother in the first week, without shame. I'd sell anything we have that's worth anything, the second car, Paolo's motorbike. And I'd do the market every Saturday and Sunday, and ask Mrs Bauer if I could sell cheese from the farm gate for her for a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I'd keep a straight face for the children, but I'd be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you mentioned Sofia's plans. Would those change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to go to university in the city. With two years, I don't know if there's anything to study for. I'd tell her to come home and learn the cheese with me, and that breaks my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having just two years change things, compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, nothing I'd planned gets time to work. The market stall is just starting. Paolo can't retrain in two years. It all lands on us at once.

S2.say: She'd say people need to pray and look after each other, because nobody in power saw it coming. She'd want the church running a food bank by spring.
S2.think: Privately she expects real trouble, with her partner's lorry job and her farm work both automated at once. Two weeks of savings and a mortgage leave no margin.
S2.do: Talks to the priest and her brother in the first week, without shame, and sells the second car and motorbike. Runs the market stall every weekend and offers to sell her employer's cheese at the farm gate for a cut.
S2.feel: Panicked, while keeping a straight face for the children.
S2.quote: I'd tell her to come home and learn the cheese with me, and that breaks my heart.
S2.fieldNote: Two exposed incomes, thin savings and no time make this her breaking point. Her instinct is faith and community, and she would drop her pride quickly. The hardest moment is changing her daughter's university plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift we should use: teach the young ones real skills, keep families close. I'd say it in church and at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough for the market stall to grow and for Paolo to find something. Not enough for us to feel safe. I'd be on edge the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Bauer to teach me everything about the cheese properly, the cultures, the ageing, so I could make it myself. I'd save every bit from the market in a separate tin. I'd push Paolo to look for local driving work with people in it, like the school bus, or train as a farrier with my cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared most days, but with something to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A farrier, at his age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's good with horses, his father kept them. My cousin Enzo is a farrier and he's always short of hands. Nobody's building a robot to hold a nervous horse's foot, not in five years anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the AI enough by then to use it for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I've seen it work for the market, yes. Sofia did my price labels with it last month and they were better than mine. I'd use it, I just wouldn't trust it with the cheese.

S3.say: She'd call five years a gift to use by teaching young people real skills and keeping families close. She'd say so in church and at the school gate.
S3.think: Privately five years is just about enough for her market stall to grow and her partner to find new work, but not enough to feel safe.
S3.do: Asks her employer to teach her cheesemaking fully and saves market income in a separate tin. Pushes her partner towards local people-facing driving or training as a farrier with her cousin.
S3.feel: Scared most days, but with something to hold onto.
S3.quote: Nobody's building a robot to hold a nervous horse's foot, not in five years anyway.
S3.fieldNote: Even with five years she stays on edge because two incomes are exposed. She builds a family plan around trusted people: her employer and her cousin. She'd use AI for the business once proven, but not for the craft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it the right way, with families and churches and apprenticeships, not just more benefits. People can learn a lot in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right, just about. Paolo could be a farrier by then, the stall could be a little business, and Sofia could finish university. But it still worries me, because the end is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the cheese fully over two or three years, and maybe one day rent a corner of the Bauers' dairy to make my own. Paolo would start with Enzo on weekends. I'd use the AI for the stall's accounts once I'm sure of it, and we'd keep Sofia's university plans as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more like the ordinary worry of a mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end is the same. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years the machines can do it all anyway. So I'm not beating them, I'm just getting my children grown before it comes. If I can get Luca to eighteen with a full belly and his faith, I've done my part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the Bauers in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be honest with me. If they're thinking of selling or buying a machine, tell me first, not after. They're good people, I think they would.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough to do it the right way, through families, churches and apprenticeships rather than more benefits. People can learn a lot in that time.
S4.think: Privately she thinks they'd just about be all right, with her partner trained as a farrier, a small cheese and chutney business and her daughter through university. She still worries because the end point is the same.
S4.do: Learns cheesemaking fully over two or three years and hopes to rent a corner of the dairy for her own cheese. Has her partner start farrier work at weekends, uses AI for the stall's accounts once sure of it, and keeps her daughter's university plans.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but more like a mother's ordinary worry.
S4.quote: If I can get Luca to eighteen with a full belly and his faith, I've done my part.
S4.fieldNote: She sees the decade as time to get her children grown rather than to beat the machines. Her plan is entirely built on community and kin. She asks only for honesty from her employers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both of us out at once, with nothing built yet. What would help is apprenticeships and local work for people Paolo's age, and help for families with children so they don't lose their homes while they start again.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the women. Everyone talks about the men's jobs, the lorry, the tractor. It's the women at the kitchen table who'll be doing the sums when the lorry doesn't come home with a wage.

headlineQuote: It's the women at the kitchen table who'll be doing the sums when the lorry doesn't come home with a wage.
portrait: Fatima Rossi is a 43-year-old junior hand on a family goat dairy and orchard farm, learning cheesemaking after years raising her children and a short stint at a supermarket counter. Her partner Paolo is a long-distance lorry driver, they have two children and a mortgage, and about two weeks saved. Traditional and churchgoing, she trusts family, church and apprenticeships more than benefits, but would take help for the children. Calm in the plateau, she grows anxious with steady change because of her partner's job, panics at two-year AGI and stays alarmed or anxious with more time while building a market stall and a farrier plan for Paolo. She sees her goal as getting her children grown before the change lands.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because she and her lorry-driver partner would both lose work at once before any plan had time to work.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and local work for people her partner's age, and help for families with children to keep their homes while they start again.
